speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the government when we may expect the report of the committee appointed to investigate the Treadgold concessions in the Yukon. There is some rumour in the press that instructions have been given to Mr. Justice Britton not to make any report at all. I assume that is inaccurate. At the same time,, it is desirable that the report, if it is to be forthcoming at all during the present session, should be before us at an early date. If I recollect correctly the statement of the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) about four or five weeks ago, it was that the report was expected early in July.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The resolution under consideration is number 89, the Intercolonial Railway, and the item is ' To equip four passenger cars with Pintsch gas apparatus, $3,500.'
We have not passed the item ' Air brakes to freight cars, $25,000.'

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: The $385,000 item and the $45,000 item were allowed to stand until Mr. Pottinger furnished ns information.
When did we pass the $25,000 item?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That was passed, then the item * To exchange draw-bars of freight cars ' stood over. Then the item * New machinery for locomotive and car shops ' was passed.

I was not aware that the $25,000 item was passed. It does not make any difference, except that the chairman' should not mark an item passed without letting the committee understand what is being done. Information was asked with regard to that, and two or three gentlemen said :. ' stand,' and I supposed it stood: I notice that sometimes these items are marked passed without the committee clearly understanding it. There should be a thorough understanding between the chairman and the committee at all times as to what is being passed.
I understood that the item respecting ' New machinery for locomotive and car shops ' and ' Air brakes to freight cars ' were to stand for certain information.
There was information asked for with regard to both. I can look up the ' Hansard ' and find out what it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I never mark an item passed unless the committee are agreeable.
The information can be brought down on another item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My clerk certifies that that item was passed. Some questions were asked in regard to it, but it was allowed to pass.

When an item is to be passed the question should be distinctly put to the committee so that every one may hear it, and that every one who has any objection to its passing or desires it to stand, may then speak. But that is not always done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I always ask ' Shall the item be adopted ? ' Then I pause for a moment or two to* see if any person objects, and if there is no response, then I declare it passed: Sometimes I may make al mistake.
Are we then to leave the items ' To strengthen bridges, $385,000 ' and ' To exchange draw-bars of freight cars, $45,000 ' to stand until we get information ?	[DOT]
Until we get information.
I think the Minister will find that some information was to be obtained about the item of $25,000.

I have asked Mr. Pot-tinger for information. This present item ' to equip four passenger cars with Pintsch gas apparatus, $3,500,' is a revote. Last year $8,000 was appropriated for the purpose. The total estimated cost for equipping the passenger ears with this apparatus is $22,400. We are asking for $3,500 in order Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
to equip four passenger cars this year. The total number to be equipped is twenty-six. Up to the 30th June, 1903, fourteen had been equipped, and it is estimated that there will have been six equipped to the 30th June last. Therefore, the estimated number that will have been equipped to the 30tli June, 1904, is twenty and the balance to be equipped after the 30th June is six. The estimated number to be done in 1904-5 is four, and after the 30th June, 1905, there will be two to be equipped.
How many cars are at present equipped ?
There are twenty-six altogether to be equipped. We have equipped twenty. That leaves six. We propose to equip four this year and two after June 30, 1905.
You do not propose to equip all your cars but only twenty-six ?
Twenty-six.
How are the other cars lighted ?
Very largely by oil.
American or Canadian ?

I could not tell the hon. gentleman; I think very largely by Canadian oil. The Imperial Oil Company have the contract for furnishing it, and as it is a Canadian concern, I presume they are furnishing good Canadian goods.
Good Standard Oil goods.
Perhaps we will have New Brunswick oil supplied before long.
I am afraid that the hon. gentleman will be endeavouring to get the contract himself in that case. Are there no cars lighted with electricity ?
No.
At one time there were. Was that abandoned altogether, and if so, why ?

I am told by the general manager that lighting by electricity proved to be entirely too expensive and that they required to use the storage battery, which had to be charged at certain points. The Pintsch gas was found to be much cheaper.

How many cars did you light with electricity ?	,
ill-. EMMERSON. We have none lighted by electricity now.
I understand you tested it. How many cars did you test it with ?
I think about ten or more were equipped and lighted with electricity, but that has all been removed.
You say ten or more. It seems to be a remarkable thing to throw away money In testing so many cars, when with one or turn you could have tested it thoroughly.

That was the method of ligthing cars that was generally used. The Intercolonial Railway in common with other railways went into the lighting of their cars with electricity. It made a very excellent light, and was a very great success, but the only drawback was the expense of it, and after it had been used for some yegrs it was taken out. The system was removed' 'five or, six years ago, Ordinary oil was used and is being used as a substitute for electricity, but oil is being replaced as far as possible in all these ears which I have mentioned by Pintsch gas.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman to state the relative cost of oil, Pintsch gas and electricity per ear ?
The general manager tells me that he has that information somewhere, but it is not available at the present moment. I can get it.
I do not want an absolutely correct answer. Could we have it stated approximately ?
The cost of electric light is about four times as great as that of Pintsch gas, with the storage battery light that was used on the Intercolonial Railway.
And as between gas and oil, what is the difference ?
Pintsch gas would cost about double as much as oil. One additional reason for using Pintsch gas is on account of the safety. The oil is very unsafe, as my hon. friend knows.
When the minister says double the cost, I presume he means the initial cost, or does he mean the cost of maintenance 5
I mean the operating cost.

The system of electric lighting used on the Canadian Pacific Railway and a great many American roads is a combination of axle and storage battery together. They sometimes have the dynamo in the baggage ear. Has this system been tried ?

The system of generating electricity from flip car itself was tried in one of the cars on the Intercolonial Railway. That was tried very generally on the Canadian Pacific Railway, but they found it to be not in the interest of the road and they discarded it almost wholly, as I am informed. Certainly they have discarded its general use in the lighting of their cars.
.	188i
Do they use Pintsch gas all through ?
Pintsch gas on some and on very many of their cars they use oil. I understand from the general manager that they have adopted acetylene gas with the Pintsch gas apparatus.
How many cars were equipped last year with Pintsch gas ?
Six up to the 30th June of the present year.
What is the cost per ear?
The cost per car is about $800.
Have you to pay a royalty on the apparatus or what is it that makes it so expensive ?
There is a contract with the Pintsch Gas Conpany and the apparatus is purchased fro: a them in New York.
May I ask what the hon. minister pays per gallon for the oil used on the road, and if the contract is let by tender ?
The contract is let by tender, but I do not know the exact figures. Tenders were called for all through Canada.
That is for illuminating oil ?
Yes. The lubricating oil would be in the mechanical department and the illuminating oil would be classified in the maintenance of way department.
How are the cars lighted on the P. E. I. Railway ?
By oil lamps.
Is it the intention to introduce the Pintsch system, which the minister says is so cheap and efficient ?
It would be very desirable to do so and it would contribute to safety.

We have a large number of tourists coming to Prince Edward Island in the summer season ; they take the train at Summerside generally in the evening and travel to Charlottetown, and they should be afforded modern accommodation on that railway. I find it very difficult myself to read a newspaper by the present lighting system. Why not introduce the Pintsch system on this evening train between Sum-merside and Charlottetown ?

We have the Pintsch system only on a limited number of cars on the main line of the Intercolonial Railroad, but now that the hon. gentleman has called my attention to this matter I shall be very glad if I can, to introduce the Pintsch system on at least one train on the Prince Edward Island Railway.
$800 per car seems a large price for introducing the Pintsch system ; one would think to look at it that it was not worth more than $150.
It is open for you to tender and I will give you a show.
I suppose there is a patent and all that. If it costs $800 a car why does the minster take $3,500 for four cars.
There are certain incidental expenses. I think the utmost care is exercised in the expenditure.
What is your policy about introducing the Pintsch system in new coaches ; I assume that it could be more cheaply done when the car is being originally constructed ?

New cars are fitted with the Pintsch system, but the expense is very largely in the cylinder and because of the length of the route of the Intercolonial Railway we have to use large cylinders to store a sufficient quantity of gas.
The minister might have 'a stronger tank and give the gas greater pressure.
That is also a question of cost and is as broad as it is long. We do the same as the other great railways and it costs us no more.
Last year you took $8,000 to fit up t.en cars ; how is it that you take more than $800 a car this year; are you paying more than last year ?
The cost is the same this year ; the difference must be due to the fact that the work on the six cars was incomplete and the revote of $3,500 is to complete the ten cars as was contemplated.
The minister stated that they are now using the acetylene apparatus for the Pintsch gas. What is the difference between the two kinds of gas ?

I think my hon. friend misunderstood me. I said that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was using acetylene gas with a Pintsch gas apparatus, and that the Intercolonial was using Pintsch gas, with Pintsch gas apparatus. There was no question of acetylene gas on the Intercolonial Railway.
What is the object of using acetylene gas with Pintsch gas apparatus? Has it been demonstrated to be better in any way?
I am informed that they tried it in a small way, and are now trying it in a larger way. It is a matter of experiment very largely, hut the results seem to be on the side of Pintsch gas.
Which would be the more injurious, in the event of gas escaping?
I have heard that the Pintsch gas is the safer and less unpleasant.
What is the material from which Pintsch gas is generated ?
It is an oil specially prepared from petroleum.
Where do you get the oil for that purpose ?
It is purchased from the Imperial Oil Company under contract, after tender.
The Imperial- Oil Company is the Canadian name of the Standard Oil Company, is it not ?
It is a Canadian company said to have some affiliation with the Standard Oil Company. I believe it is the Canadian Standard.
That is generally imported oil ?

No, they have their refinery at Sarnia, I think. They import a certain class of crude petroleum which is not produced in Canada and which they blend with Canadian oils. I know they do that with respect to their lubricants.
The hon. gentleman must admit that the Imperial Oil Company is a branch of the Standard Oil Company?

The Standard Oil Company has a great many divisions. It is recognized in Canada as the Standard Oil Company of Canada, but I understand that it has a great many Canadian shareholders. In fact, it was a Canadian company consisting of Canadian capitalists, and it affiliated with the Standard. That is my information. I have no personal knowledge of the matter.

The hon. minister asks for '$35,000 for installing this system of lighting the cars and charges it to capital account. He has already charged to capital account the system which was used before. This is uot fair or right.

Mbst of the cars which have been changed in that way were lighted by the ordinary oil lamps. It is a good many years since the Intercolonial had in use electric lighting. Most of the cars in which that was used have since departed and have been replaced by modern cars. For instance, those used on the Maritime express and on the new Ocean Limited train, which was initiated this week, are all equipped as they are purchased from the manufacturers. So that it is only with respect to the cars which have been lighted with ordinary oil lamps and on which the Pintsch gas system is being installed, that we are charging the cost to capital account.
Where are the cars made ?
Some are made at Amherst and some at Cobourg.
Are any imported ?

Yes, the sleepers have heretofore been almost wholly imported. I am in hopes, however, that with the completion of certain works in Canada, we shall hereafter be in a position to secure our pullmans in Canada.

1 do not think the answer which the minister has given covers the matter satisfactorily. The electric lighting system, which was formerly in a large number of cars, was charged to capital account; and he is throwing that out and putting in this new system and charging the whole expense to capital account. This item should be struck out.

I am sorry not to be able to satisfy my hon. friend. I am trying to give him the information as it is. When the electric lighting system was tried some years ago, it was merely an experiment. As it did not prove advantageous or economical, the department decided to change it. As the electric system cost four times as much as the Pintsch gas system, it is certainly in the interest of the country that the change should be made; and the other being an experiment, and this being an improvement, whereby a great saving will be effected, it seems to me that this should be charged to capital account.

The hon. minister has mistaken the argument entirely. What he says and what the hon. minister says is that some of these cars were lighted by electricity before. That was charged to capital account. My hon. friend has no objection to substituting a better light, but what he is objecting to is that having charged the other to capital account you substitute another and perhaps a better light and charge it to capital account. He has no objection to the change whatever, but he asks why you charge it to capital account.

If it were tried as an experiment at the expense of capital account and it proved to be a failure and not in the interest of the road surely the revenue account should not suffer thereby. It has proved to be such a failure that it is practi-ally worthless and it should be a capital expenditure now in substituting Pintsch gas.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me the difference in the capital account between the 1st of July this year and the 1st July last year ?

I presume my hon. friend (Mr. Rosamond) is familiar with the capital expenditure up to the 30th June,
1902. The information I gave to the House last evening was that the total capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway up to the 30th June, 1903 w'as $70,523,360.43. If he will deduct $2,216,744.88 from these figures he will have the total capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway up to the 30th June, 1902.
What I want to get at is the increase in the expenditure on capital account since the 30tli June, 1903 ?

I have not those figures.
I will get that information as soon as I possibly can.

The capital account is going on increasing from year to year while the value of the road is not increasing proportionately. A great deal of the expenditure, such as that which has been referred to by my hon. friend on my right (Mr. Clancy), ought to be charged to the ordinary7 expenditure for the regular running expenses of the road. But, the hon. minister, following the practice of previous ministers, has tried to make his deficit less by charging to capital expenditure what ought to go to ordinary current account. This is a deception on the public which ought not to be continued any longer.

The committee is somewhat anxious to be enlightened as to where the hon. minister draws the line, if he has any line to draw, between capital and consolidated expenditure. First of all I understand these cars are fitted with oil lamps. Next follows an electric apparatus and that is followed by lamps. I say lamps because the hon. gentleman says that it is some years ago since the experiment was tried. This has been followed by the Pintsch gas apparatus and he charges all of it to capital account. Where is the hon. gentleman going to end and where does he commence ? What constitutes the proper working expenses of the road if that be the case ? The hon. gentleman said that it was an experiment. Are capital expenditures to be based absolutely on the merits of the experiment, on what it may turn out to be afterwards? That seems to be the hon. gentleman's main excuse, for taking that course. I am sure that the committee is anxious, especially as the hon. gentleman has come newly into that department, that the country may know that the deception that my hon. friend from Lanark (Mi*. Rosamond) has pointed out consists in this: that the hon. gentleman is charging everything to capital account which has absolutely no value. If a failure, it is charged to capital account, when it should represent some value in the road afterwards. I am not going so far as to say that such a thing is possible always but that should be one of the main objects. The hon. gentleman unloads every expenditure for trifling changes upon capital account when the fact is that it should be

charged to working expenses. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will explain the multiplicity of transitions from one state of things to another wherein he is unloading all these expenditures on capital account.

It is a much disputed question as to what should be charged to capital account and what to revenue, but I think I should take issue with my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Rosamond) when he states that the capital account has been increased and that the road is not increasing in value. I think it must be recognized that the Intercolonial Railway is very much more valuable this year than it was last.
To the country or to the party ?

Yes, to the country and to the railway itself-a very much more valuable railway. When my hon. friend from North Lanark states that it is lessened in value I am sure he is simply making an argument which will not hold water.
I do not think I said ' lessened in value.'
I understood my hon. friend to say that. At all events he said that it had not increased in value. Perhaps those were the words he used.
I said it had not increased in value in proportion to the extra expenditure charged to capital account.
I understood him to make no qualification in respect to it. I dispute the statement. I say it has been increasing in value.
Why do you dispute a statement which has not been made ?
One at a time, please.

I want to ask the hon. minister, if he will allow me, why he challenges a statement that my hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Rosamond) said he never made ? It is very ingenious but there is not much sense in it.

I have not challenge.! the statement of my hon. friend from North Lanark when he says ' increased ' instead of [DOT] lessened.' I accept that statement; I am not disputing the thing ; I am simply pointing out that in my judgment the road has very materially improved by reason of these capital expenditures, because we have better equipment, we have larger engines and we have heavier rails. But in determining the question as to whether we should charge an appliance of this kind to capital account or not, I would ask my hon. friend from Both-well (Mr. Clancy) this question : Suppose that the road had been originally equipped with a certain cattle-guard, that that cattle-guard was becoming inoperative because of use, without being worn out or destroyed, that it was found to be not in the interest Mr. CLANCY.
cf the railway, that it had to be entirely discarded, that within a year after the construction of the road you substitute a modern cattle-guard, one that would be accepted, -would you charge the substituted appliance to capital or to current account ? I hold that if you charge the original cattle-guard to capital account the substituted article should be so charged also, because the cattle-guard is not replaced because of wear and tear, it is not replaced because of destruction by accident, but it is replaced because it has proved a failure, it having been an experiment, true at the expense of capital account, but the substituted article should also be charged to the same account. These are my views. I understand that this is a much debated question, not merely in this House, but in private corporations. Some hold one view and others hold another.
(Intercolonial Railway-To equip passenger cars with vestibules, $4,000.
The hon. gentleman ha3 selected a very extreme case.

It is a parallel case.
Mr. CLANCY'. I will, however, take the case of cattle-guards which he has suggested. I imagine if cattle-guards were to be changed under existing conditions on the Intercolonial they would not all be changed in one year. They have been in use many years, and they have served a certain purpose during that period ; and what would follow in a business of that kind, as in ail ethers, is that they would be changed when they were worn out. There is a life in the use of a cattle-guard, and it must be changed at some time, even if it is not remodelled. Now, if you put in new cattle-guards, the most that would be charged to capital account would be the difference between the new kind and what the old ones would cost. Let me ask the hon. gentleman this question :	If a cattle-guard had reached the
stage in its history when it became dangerous to the road and needed to be repaired in the public interest, and when he proposed to put in a new sort of cattle-guard that had not been in use before, would he charge the whole of that sum to capital account, or 'merely the difference between the cost of the old cattle-guard and the cost of the new one ? To what account would he charge the expenditure in that case ?

That is an entirely different case to the one under discussion.
T make a distinction as between a cattle-guard that became inoperative or worn out and another one introduced as an experiment. But I would call the attention of the committee that the item under discussion is for furnishing four passenger cars with Pintsch gas apparatus. These four ears today are equipped with ordinary oil lamps ; there is no electric lighting equipment. We propose putting in each of these four cars an appliance to use Pintsch gas. That is

the question in this item. It does not involve a substitution of Pintseh gas for electric light, but it simply involves putting an additional appliance on that car to enable us to operate it with greater safety and ad vantage to the travelling public.
Are you not substituting one kind of light by another ! .

True, but you would not say that it should be charged to current account when you are only improving the character of the car. The question is whether you would deduct from that charge the cost of the oil lamp.
To equip passenger! cars with vestibules, $4,000.

This is a revote. Last year $10,000 was asked for this purpose, and six cars were equipped. It costs about $1,000 to equip a car with a vestibule. We now propose to equip four cars, and four more in 1905. That makes a total of twenty cars, all that we contemplate equipping now.
Is that done by day labour ?
By day labour in the shops at Moncton.
Then how do you get the $4,000, when it is done by day labour.
The labour done in connection with this is charged up against this particular item.
An estimate of the labour and the material used.

They keep a very' accurate account of the labour. A certain number of men are put on this particular work and their wages are charged up against the appropriation for that particular item.
Intercolonial	Railway-Additional sidings
along the line, $118,000.
I would ask the minister to explain this item. Last year there was a good deal of discussion about a similar item and the next item, for increased accommodation and facilities along the line.
I do not think that this committee would want all these particular items set forth in the estimates.
Speaking for myself I do.
It takes all kinds of people to make up the world and I presume all kinds of people to make up the committee.
I appreciate that and that is why I asked the question.

We are asking for $118,000. There is a siding one half mile east of Christmas Island. This proposed siding is to hold 40 cars. It is a crossingsiding where trains can meet, and it is estimated that it will cost $4,000. Christmas Island is in Cape Breton.
ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) It is just beyond the Strait of Canso, within three miles of the Grand Narrows, after crossing the bridge.
At Alba there is a proposed extension of a siding and it is estimated the cost will be $2,000.
ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) That is In Inverness county.
Will the minister give an estimate of the amount in each case and why it is charged to capital account ?

All of these sidings are proposed on account of the larger engines now' in use ; on account of the greater number of cars that we are enabled to haul the sidings have been found to be entirely too short for safety of the road, and for convenience in the moving of trains and it is found necessary to have these extensions.
The minister said yesterday that he did not use the heavy locomotives and long trains in Cape Breton at all.
We are not using the heaviest but we are using heavier engines.
You told the House yesterday that on the New Glasgow' and Cape Breton branches of the road you did not intend to make any changes because you u'ere not using the heavy locomotives.

I meant that the heaviest class of locomotives such as are on the trunk line between Halifax and Montreal are not in use there, but there is a heavier class than has been in use and longer trains are being hauled on the New Glasgow branch and the Cape Breton section than has been the case heretofore, necessitating extended sidings.
At Brierly's Brook, in Antigonish, it is estimated that the extension of the siding will cost $1,500. At Merigomish, in Pictou county, there is required an extension of a siding of 250 feet w'hich is estimated to cost $000. Between Glengarry and Hopewell they want a crossing siding to hold 50 cars and it is estimated to cost $4,000. At Lans-downe they require a siding to hold 20 cars w'hich is estimated to cost $1,500. What is the total amount which will be required to dredge out this rock and how much has been expended ?

It is to provide for 30 feet.
Throughout the dock limits ?
Within the dock limits.

One of the piers there is not in good condition, but this dredging will give 30 feet of water over an area within which five of the largest ships can lie at low tide.
Intercolonial Railway-Improvements at Little Metis station and diverting public road, $4,000.

Everybody knows that Little Metis is a favourite summer resort. The situation of the station was such that tourists getting off there, day or night, were compelled to cross the track, go away around, and then go over another level crossing, thereby increasing the distance to their destination and at the same time exposing them to a certain amount of danger. I am not personally familiar with the place, except by having seen it in passing' on the train. But to afford proper accommodation for the station, and convenience to the travelling public, passengers as well as freight, we propose to purchase some land near the main highway, and build a station on the same side, thereby enabling tourists and others frequenting that resort to get to that point with less travel and greater safety to themselves.
Why was not this amount expended last year ? The minister says now this expenditure was greatly needed. At the same time he might tell us what the $15 was expended for.	.

I do not know that X am familiar with the expenditure of the $15. But my hon. friend is probably aware of the fact that the people who frequent that resort live on the shore in one parish, and that the people residing near the station, or on the land where the station is situated, are in another parish. It was proposed by the railway officials that the municipality at the station should give a right of way, recognizing as the officials did that this would be of advantage to the place and an advantage to that municipality as well. But the municipality did not see it in that light, and therefore negotiations took place between the department and the representatives of the municipality, with the result that we could not agree. The matter was flnally referred to myself, and I decided that it should not be delayed any longer, that it should be determined, and that if these people would not provide the right of way the railway should provide it.

Can my hon. friend give some details of the negotiations that were carried on between the municipal councils and the Railway Department ? I think that the municipality where the strangers go in summer is St. Octave, and the station is called Little Mfitis. Now' with which municipal council w'as the department negotiating with, and what steps were taken to reach a solution of the difficulty ?

I think the land which the road traverses is in St. Octave and the other is Little Metis. A dispute arose between the officials of St. Octave and the Railway Department, and not w'ith the people of Little Metis. Would my hon. friend give some details of the negotiations that w-ere carried on w'ith the municipal council of St. Octave ? Where did they break off ?

The negotiations with St. Octave were carried on through the mayor of Little Metis, Mr. Ferguson, I think his name is. The negotiations were carried on through him, with the result that certain resolutions w-ere passed by the municipalities respectively. These came before the officials, but with no result. Nothing having been done, the matter was recently referred to me, and we concluded that we had better end the strife and change the road in the interest of the travelling public and of the rallw'ay.

I suppose that if there are no elections held this year we will revote this sum next year.
Intercolonial Railway-New station at Windsor, N.S., &e., $10,000.

We want an explanation of this. Last year the item for this station read as follows :

New station at Windsor, N.S., provided that the railway companies using the station make arrangements satisfactory to the Governor in Council for payment by way of interest or rental of a reasonable proportion of the cost, $10,000. .

This is simply a revote. There was some questions as to the company entering into a suitable arrangement with respect to the use of the station. But in the meantime the necessity for a station at Windsor is very great.
Who occupies this station ?
There are only two roads that occupy it, the Dominion Atlantic and the Midland. The Intercolonial owns the Windsor branch, but it is under lease to the Dominion Atlantic.

When the vote is not accompanied with the qualification which is to be observed in the estimate of last year, that would seem to indicate either that the qualification has been abandoned, or that satisfactory arrangements have been made. Which alternative does the minister present to us ?

I do not wish to have it understood that the Intercolonial abandons the position it has taken with respect to this matter. But I think it is fair to place the railway management in a position whereby, if the conditions absolutely require it, they may provide station accommodation there without being subjected to any hindrance from any other quarter. But so far as the attitude of the Intercolonial is concerned in relation to this matter, and with regard to the Dominion Atlantic, the Intercolonial does not recede one iota from the attitude which it has held heretofore.

Although the vote is not accompanied with any condition such as we had last year, we understand that the policy of the department appears to be in the same position as ir was last year. Is that right ?
That is the view which the department feels called upon to take.

There are two reasons why this work was not commenced. One was the lateness of the season at which the vote was passed. It was not desirable that the work should be commenced late last fall. Another was that no arrangement had been made with the Dominion Atlantic, and Intercolonial Railway was not disposed to recede from its position. As to the total cost it is supposed that $10,000 will provide a suitable station at that place.
What do the Midland Railway Company pay for the use of that station ?

They do not pay the Intercolonial Railway anything. They pay the Dominion Atlantic.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. The length of the session last year has been put forward by the hon. minister as a reason for not proceeding with some of these works which were described as very urgent and necessary. For example we were told last year that the present station at Windsor was so absolutely inadequate that it should not be taken into consideration in determining whether or not this expenditure should all be charged to capital account. If that be the correct position it must be a very poor station indeed. My recollection is that in August or early in September, we voted one fifth of every item in the estimates without discussion in order that the business of the country might not be hindered and that the construction of these public works might not be delayed. Yet we are told by the hon. minister that the length of the session has prevented anything whatever from being done. I would like some explanation of that.

While it is true there was a vote of a certain percentage, it was for the purposes of the financial department rather than for the purposes of any of the special departments of government and not having reference to the arrangement of work. While that is true, several departments of the government could not very well understand what should be done until these special votes went through parliament. The Intercolonial officials acted upon that principle. Unfortunately the general manager was obliged to be here the greater jtor-tion of the year until the latter end of October, and some of the engineers were here also in connection with the estimates before parliament. Then it was about the 1st of November before any of this work could be mapped out and arrangements made for it, and they found that to be entirely too late. The enhanced cost of doing work at that season of the year justifies delay where possible. But, a very strong element in respect to this Windsor Station I am bound to say was what was deemed to be the unfair position-perhaps I should not use that word certainly what was deemed to be a position that was not in harmony with what the Intercolonial Railway wanted-taken by the Dominion Atlantic Company. The negotiations have not been satisfactory. I do not speak personally in respect to the matter never having been drawn into it, but the general manager has felt that they were not willing to meet the Intercolonial Railway in the way they should.

The Dominion At-1 lantic has a lease from the government of

the line from Windsor Junction to Windsor and also a lease of running powers. from Windsor Junction to Halifax, as I understand it, and the rental is based on a certain proportion of the gross earnings. As a part of the terms of the lease the government is required to maintain the road. I suppose the maintenance of the road will involve the keeping up of the station. Of course, I recognize that at Windsor the line owned by the Dominion Atlantic joins the line owned by the Crown and which is leased to the Dominion Atlantic. What is the scheme

you already have ?

This vote will complete the whole work ?

To enlarge the yard and provide additional sidings ; improve and level lumber yards ; grade the grounds ; enlarge cattle pens ; provide two additional standpipes including waterpipes and connections, and to improve and enlarge the station.

Surely there must be an end to this enormous expenditure. Has the minister no pity for the poor ratepayers of Canada-asking $1,651,000 on capital account this year ; a deficit on the running account of the Intercolonial Railway for ten months of last year of $545,000 ; a charge on capital account for ten months of $1,000,000 ; a charge on capital account on the Prince Edward Island road of $6,000 or $7,000, and we do not know what the deficit on the Prince Edward Island road is ? We don't want any more government roads.

Not if they are managed as the Intercolonial Railway is. M by are you asking for this enormous expenditure ? You should ask for nothing this year except for what is absolutely necessary for the road. Is the House going to submit to this ; is the country going to submit to it; and especially as I am reminded by an lion, friend that you are going to build another line from the Atlantic to the Pacific ?

rattle along and the trains to run In a go-as-you-please-manner ; and we could permit the road-bed to get into a condition which [DOT]would not be creditable to us. But in order to keep it up to its present efficiency ; and in order to provide accommodation all along the road and to meet the demands of the traffic ; we have to make this expenditure. For instance there is no more thriving town in this Dominion than the town of Amherst. There is no place where the manufacturers are progressing and advancing to a greater extent. I do not happen to have the honour of representing the town ; it is very worthily represented by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) whose modesty will not permit him to mention his own name.
Or come ba'ck to the House.

Just outside of Hal-ton. Halton covers most of the earth and Amherst is included in what is left on the fringe. The trade of the Intercolonial Railway demands this vote, and I do not think there is any occasion for the outburst of my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart), but probably he was not as serious as he looked. I trust he will feel that we are doing our best for the Intercolonial Railway
account, just after there has been a deficit of $1,700,000.

It is delicious to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) speaking in this manner about the Intercolonial Railway. Now, the hon. minister is endeavouring to improve the Intercolonial Railway. Everybody who has travelled in the maritime provinces knows that in 1896 the railway was almost producing grass on its roadbed. To-day it is being made an up-to-date road. The item under discussion is for increased accommodation for the town of Amherst. I may say that the freight receipts of the town of Amherst, when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) was Minister of Railways, amounted to less than $75,000, whereas this year they have amounted to $247,000. Are we to mark time ? Are the accommodations for freight that only brings $75,000 to be equal to the accommodations for freight that brings a quarter of a million ? The industries of the town of Amherst have developed with remarkable strides under the present administration and the present tariff. Take one industry alone, in the vicinity of the station. The firm of Rhodes, Curry & Co. in 1896 was doing a business of only $425,000 a year, and employed less than 300 men. Last year the same firm did a business of $2,700,000 and employed 900 men in their home

Let me tell the hon. gentleman that It was not a rattletrap road in 1896. The road was kept in excellent condition in 1896. manufactory, and 400 or 500 in other places. Our freight has been lying on the sidewalks for want of room in the freight sheds ; our sidings have been jammed full of cars, with insufficient [DOT]means for shunting ; and the hon. minister is doing only the proper thing, which should have been done three years ago, in providing this increased accommodation. The remarks I made had reference, not to Amherst, but to the whole vote.
The greater includes the less.

Yes, the greater includes the less. I am delighted, as everyone else must be. at the increased business at Amherst. We avish the whole business of the Intercolonial Railway would in-

crease at a like rate, and that there would be an end to the deficits. The hon. minister will not increase the rates on the road ; he says the people of the country will not submit to any increase. We have, then, to submit patiently to a loss of between $2,000,000 and $2,500,000 a year for the purpose of keeping the Intercolonial Railway running. That railway could be run without any loss whatever, and kept up to its present standard. These expenditures for sidings, deep water termini, and many other things are interminable, and are not justifiable at all. The whole surplus earnings of the Dominion government up to last year were expended on the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, and the payment of the deficits. Nearly all the surpluses of the government up to last year were dropped into that sinkhole. Last year the amount on the Intercolonial alone was $2,300,000, and this year it is $1,800,000. I do not know what it is on the other roads.

The remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) discredited the management of that road more than anything that has been said on this side of the House. He speaks of the enormous increase that has taken jfiace ,n the receipts at the town of Amherst. If there is anything like that increase in the earnings of the road, that fact is a great condemnation of its management generally. There must be something radically wrong with it. Either they are carrying freight and passengers at altogether too little, or it is costing a great deal too much to carry them. Hon. gentlemen must take either horn of the dilemma. They cannot keep on bragging that they are increasing the traffic of that road unless they show that they are getting a little nearer to making it self-supporting. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has often stated in this House that that road could be made self-sustaining. If the same rates were charged on the Intercolonial that are charged on other roads In this country, we would not have the tremendous deficits which we are confronted with from year to year. If the hon. member for Cumberland would try to help the government instead of criticising them so severely as he has done to-day, he might do some good. The statement that that road was in a ramshacle condition in 1895-96 is not in accordance with the facts. Compared with other roads at that time, it was pronounced by eminent engineers to be the best road in the country.
Will the hon. gentleman name the eminent engineers ?

It is not necessary. The deputy minister will know very well who the eminent engineers are. I state as a 189*
fact that that road, in its roadbed and its equipment, was the best road in the country at that time ; and in that shape it was handed over to the present government Yet hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were on this side of the House, condemned the late government for their expenditures on the road. There is a grave suspicion that the Intercolonial Railway is doing business largely for the benefit of the local traffic, at a very low rate, and that that low rate is the reason for the very serious deficits which occur year after year. Now that the present Minister of Railways and Canals has taken charge, we have a right to expect much better things from his great experience in these matters. If he will see that proper rates are charged, some of these deficits might be saved to the country.

So far as this particular item is concerned, I regard it as perhaps less subject to criticism than any other item among those we are discussing. The itown of Amherst undoubtedly has made very great progress during the last ten years. I would not be inclined to attribute that progress exactly to the causes mentioned by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan). I would attribute it rather to the business enterprise of the people, and their great capacity in developing their industries. I believe the town of Amherst has almost doubled its population, perhaps quite doubled it, within the time 1 have mentioned. Undoubtedly the output of the manufacturing establishments of the town has enormously increased during that period ; but that is owing to the general prosperous conditions which have prevailed throughout the world, and more especially to the remarkable ability and enterprise of the people who are engaged in those enterprises in that particular town. I believe the accommodation at Amherst is inadequate at the present time, and I for one am very glad indeed to support the vote of $15,000 for giving better accommodation. Not only is there the great manufacturing establishment of Rhodes, Curry & Co., but half a dozen others which might be named. There are the Robb Manufacturing Company, which manufactures engines of all kinds, the Amherst Boot and Shoe Company, and a number of other enterprising and prosperous concerns, which are continually turning in very large amounts of freight to the Intercolonial Railway.
Undoubtedly if the traffic along the whole route of the Intercolonial had developed in anything like the proportion shown in the town of Amherst, there would be a very different condition of affairs presented from that which the hon. minister submits to us. I believe that fihe road should be kept up to a very high standard, and when my hon. friend from Cumberland says it Was not so kept up in days gone by, he probably forgets that when we purchased the Drummond County Railway, some two years after the

present government came into power, the Intercolonial was held up as a standard of the highest excellence, and the argument used was that the Drummond County road, with a comparatively small expenditure, could be brought up to the standard of the Intercolonial.
; Mr. LOGAN. That is the standard of the roadbed.

I would like to point out the fact that the Intercolonial is seriously discriminated against in the purchase of its coal. Tlie Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway purchase their coal delivered in Montreal cheaper than the Intercolonial can purchase its coal in Sydney, Pictou and Cumberland. The local consumers in eastern Canada are likewise discriminated against. There is certainly a remedy which could be applied. 'If certain large and valuable coal areas were taken hold of and worked by the gov-lernment, we could get coal as cheap as other railways and the eastern consuming population would get it at a price probably 50 cents per ton cheaper than now.

I cannot allow the statement of my hon. friend to go unchallenged. On certain occasions I have had the opportunity of going very carefully into the coal sales of the different large coal corporations -in Nova Scotia, and I can prove that the average price charged the Intercolonial is less than the price charged private consumers in the maritime provinces or anywhere else. The coal companies of Nova Scotia 'have been able to increase the rate paid the miners of that province the last few years by over twenty per cent, and they cannot be expected to sell coal as cheaply as in days gone by. This is a railway bridge on the line between Point Tupper and Sydney. It separates the two arms of the Bras d'Or lake. Th's is a draw bridge, and vessels pass through it carrying large quantities of marble and lime stone for the Sydney works. Barges also carry this material through this drawbridge. The current is so swift and it strikes the bridge at such a peculiar angle that it is with great danger not only to vessels but to the bridge itself that the passage is attempted. Now an attempt has been made to direct that current, and in order that the vessels may pass through there with safety not only to themselves but to the bridge, this became essential. Some men who have studied these matters were sent there with the engineers and they have suggested a remedy. It is proposed to have an extension of the crib 200 feet long, 24 feet wide at the top, 15 wide at the bottom and 72 feet high. T'he water is very deep there. In my opinion the Minister of Railways lias not pursued a constitutional course in this matter. We voted $10,000 last year for a specific purpose, the object of which was explained to us. It was said that this $10,000 would complete the object, and the committee was pledged last year to a total expenditure of $10,000, whereas now we are pledged to a total expenditure of $80,000, and the $10,000 voted last year has been appropriated, without authority I believe, to this new scheme. I have earned a very good reputation for not speaking too much and I would not wish to destroy it by going to the other extreme ; but if the committee will pardon me I will explain. This bridging of the Grand Narrows, the connecting link of northern and western portion of Cape Breton with the southern and eastern portion is a very important matter. If anything happened to that swing or drawbridge, the whole traffic of the Sydneys would be interrupted. Protests were made against the old plan by the business interests of Sydney who represented that if that cluster of piles were put down there would be danger not only to the vessels but to the bridge as well, because, should the currents swing these vessels against the draw there would be a complete interruption of traffic. As the responsible head of the department I
did not think that any risk should be taken and as this $10,000 was entrusted to the Department of Railways to overcome the difficulties at that point, and without there being any plan or specification for carrying on a particular work, I do not think parliament would wish that the old design should be carried out, if it were found that it should not accomplish the good intended. No advantage has been taken of parliament by the action of the Railway Department, because the money was voted for the purpose of removing the difficulty and danger at that point, and it has been devoted to that purpose.
