Now I would like to ask the minister if the men of Prince Edward Island who are engaged on this work have not the strength, the physique and the appearance of any men employed on the Intercolonial, and why are they not entitled to $1.25 or $1.30 a day? Having placed these men on that work at $1 a day, as he will find in his reports and as he stated in this House in answer to a question, he will simply be doing an injustice to the men of Prince Edward Island if he does not increase their wages to $1.25 per day.

I will say to my hon. friend that the regular employees along the line of the Prince Edward Island Railway, the trackmen and the section foremen, are paid by the same schedule as are the men on the Intercolonial. I am not aware of the amount paid last winter for the particular

work to which the hon. gentleman referred but if they were paid at that rate, it was because they worked very short hours, the teams employed in hauling the 'stuff were only employed during Abe winter days, and the men necessarily did not work a full day. They were only paid in accordance with the work they were performing.
Why was it necessary to fill in this hole at that particular time 1
This stuff had to be hauled across the harbour or river, it had to be hauled before the ice broke up. and this place had to be filled up.

We 'have had winters for the past thirty years and we have had ice, and certainly if this hole required to be filled up it could have been done any time within the past thirty years. But the minister is more enterprising apparently than the ministers who have gone before him. Now this little place at Charlottetown is well known to everybody.
That little place was only recently purchased.
It has been in the hands of the government for the past thirty years, as their property.
That isthc local government.	[DOT]
No. the federal government.

I am informed that this property only recently became the property of the railway, within a very few months, and that previously it was owned by the provincial government of Prince Edward Island. The railway had nothing whatever to do with it. The work required to be done during the winter months, but the summer came on before the ice broke up, and the department found it necessary to commence this work immediately. The fact that an election was coming on was not a sufficient reason for delaying the work.

I know all about this business. That little corner between the railway and the gas house at Charlottetown has been overflowed with water for the last thirty years. It is the property of the federal government, and every year the sleepers bought bv this government for the purpose of the track on the Island railway were thrown in there to be saturated with salt water in order that they might last longer. The hon. gentleman will find out that this is correct if he will consult his general manager who is beside him.
I get my information from him.

I know all about it. On
the eve of a by-election in March last, it was found necessary to close up this place to throw brush and stones into it in order that
a certain number of people in Charlottetown might be employed in government work, and that their votes might be thus controlled by the government.
If it was only brush and stone, it was not dust thrown in their eyes.

No. it was not dust, it was snow and ice. Surely the minister will understand that after this hole had remained there for thirty years there was no other reason for filling it up but the fact of a by-election coming on so that the government could control a few voters.
Prince Edward Island Railway-To enlarge freight shed at Breadalbane, $500.

The requirements of Phis place < all for a much larger freight
shed. $500 is the total estimated cost.
Prince Edward Island Railway-To lit up locomotives and passenger cars for steam heating-$14,500.
We require to fit up [DOT]*7 locomotives for steam heating at a cost of $75 each, and 61 passenger cars at a cost of $200 each. The total estimated cost is $14,225. .
How are these cars heated now ?- -
With an ordinary stove. This vote will heat all the passenger cars. It is proposed to appropriate the whole amount this year, and we expect the work will be finished during the fiscal year.
Is it done by tender 1
It is done by mechanics in the repair shops.
Are there any cars at present heated by steam from the engine in Prince Edward Island '!

Not on the Island.
Prince Edward Island Railway-To apply M. C. B. couplers to rolling stock, $26,500.

This is to apply the standard coupler to the rolling stock. We propose to apply it to 22 locomotives at a cost of $25 each, to 61 passenger cars at a cost of $70 each, and to 413 freight cars at a cost of $50 each.
For a coupler ?
For a coupler.
How many are there on the Intercolonial Railway not equipped with the coupler ?
There are none on the Intercolonial Railway.
Are all on the Intercolonial Railway equipped with a coupler ?

Almost all have been equipped. There is a vote in the estimates now for the purpose. Ten snow ploughs. $50 each, and flangers. $50 each, making the sum total required $26,500.

'Prince Edward Island Railway

Murray Har-obur branch and Hillsboro bridge, $650,000.
Mould the hon. gentleman explain this ? [DOT]

Last year there was a vote of $1,230,000. Of that down to June 30, 1904, it is estimated that the expenditure was $580,000. That leaves $650,000 to be revoted. The matter was very fully discussed at the last session of parliament. I can go into the details again if the members of the committee wish.
I would like to know how far the work has progressed, what remains to be done, and if this will finish it ? I remember the discussion that took place last year.

The work is under construction now. It is expected it will be completed early this fall. I think the time for the completion of -the work is December 30. The construction is going on, and I think going on quite rapidly now.
How far have they got ?
I think the whole line is graded down to Murray Harbour.
What is the length of the whole line ?

Fifty miles.
Mr. WrILlSON. I would like to ask whether the contract was let by tender, and if the work is under contract at the present time ?

Yes ; a certain proportion of the line was originally -put up to tender. Then the contractor, Mr. McManus, through an affliction, was unable to proceed, and it was determined not to accept his tender. I think in that we acted very wisely in all interests. A contract was entered into with Mr. Willard Kitchen, one of the tenderers. An extension of the contract was entered into then for the whole line at his figures down to Murray Harbour and he is completing the work now. I think he is on the last six and a half miles.

I do not know the reason why the contract was taken from the first contractor, but if it was taken from him T do not see why you did not ask for tenders to finish the job, instead of letting it to another contractor by private contract.
The contract was not entered into witli Mr. McManus at all, but the other tender was taken.
Was the other tender a larger one than Mr. McManus' tender ?
Yes, it was.
By how much ?

There was very little difference, but there were very excellent reasons on the ground of the health of the party tendering, why the tender should not be accepted. There were special reasons given at the time, and as a result the other tender was accepted.
Perhaps the hon. minister will tell us why there were two tenders asked for. Did you ask for tenders from turn different contractors ? How did Mr. McManus come to be connected with it ?
He was one of the tenderers.
Was he the lowest !
He was the lowest.
Was the contract awarded to him ?
It was not awarded to him. because the department thought it would not be wise to accept his tender and to entrust the work .to him because of his condition of health.
They do not always take the lowest tender, do they ?

Unless there are exceptional reasons. I want to say that Mr McManus is a very great personal and political friend of my own, but his tender was not accepted for very good reasons in his own interest, and, as I believe, in the interest of the department, because I am sure it would never have done to have had the work carried on by him at that time.
Was there a separate tender for the bridge, and if so, at what rate ?
There was a separate tender.
What was the bridge to cost ? Give us a little information at least as to what the tender was for the rest of it.
The tenders were made up on the basis of schedule prices. There was not a lump sum quoted for the work, but there were prices quoted for works specifically required.
But the engineers certainly, if there were schedule prices, gave the minister their estimate of the cost of the bridge

The estimated cost of the bridge is $1,494,097 ; the estimated cost of the branch to the river, $926,460 ; the estimated cost of rolling stock, $200,000 [DOT] the estimated cost of the extension to the harbour, $104,600 ; and the estimated cost of the cribwork wharf at the harbour, $69.955, making a total estimated cost of $2,795,113.17. Of that we have paid, including the estimated expenditure for 1903-4, $2,072,525.47. We will require for 1904-5 $722 -587.70. We take a vote of $650,000 for next year.
What will be the tota cost of the work including the bridge ?
Why does not the minister ask for enough money to complete the work ?
We did not wish to ask parliament for more than would be required in that time.
Is it expected that the i *work will be finished during the fiscal year ?
It may not be found necessary to finish the crib-work wharf.
Will this complete the work ?
What is the total amount of the contract ?

The estimated total amount of the contract including the wharf is $2,795,113.17. There has been expended and paid for up to date including the estimated payments for the year ending 30th of June last, $2,072,525.47. That will leave a balance of $722,5S7.70, and in the main estimates we ask for $650,000. The wharf is a matter which is to be determined. The contract is such that we need not build it unless we deem it necessary.
Am I to understand that on the highway portion of the bridge no tolls will be paid.

The provincial government is contributing the interest on the cost of that part of that bridge which is used as a highway, and I *understand that they have a statute under which they can collect tolls.

What is the arrangement between the local government and the federal government as regards that ; it ought be a free bridge if possible. It seems strange that the local government should be able to collect tolls on a bridge which we are building. I have strong objection to tolls, because we suffer a great deal from that antiquated system in the city of Montreal. How does it come, that the local government, by virtue of a lodal statute can collect tolls on a bridge which we are constructing.

I would impress upon the minister the importance of having a free bridge. In these modern days there should be no tolls on any highway in Canada. Years ago we abolished them on the highways of the riding which I have the honour to represent.

We are retrograding v hen we ask the people of Prince Edward Island to pay tolls when crossing over this bridge. I agree with my hon. friends from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) in their condemnation of tolls. Is the work on that bridge going on at the present time ?

I do not think that lion, gentlemen opposite are justified in assuming that the local government will charge tolls on this bridge. I would point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that the federal government is not bearing the whole cost of this bridge ; the local government
is contributing the interest on the cost of that portion of it which will be used as a highway.
To whom is the interest being paid by the local government ?
To the federal government when the bridge will be in operation. I presume it may be deducted from the provincial subsidies.
My hon. friend does hot know exactly what the terms of the arrangement are.
I know in a general way.
I understood the minister to say that the provincial government was entitled to collect tolls, that does not coincide with the statement of my hon. friend.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) said that the federal government was providing the whole cost of that bridge. .
There is no doubt of that; my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) admits it.'
In one sense that would be right, but if the local government are paying the interest on a portion of the cost of the bridge, that portion would belong to them.

My hon. friend assumes that because the local government are going to pay interest on the highway portion of the bridge, they will own that portion. I do not understand why they should. On the contrary', I think we _shall own it ourselves.

I think to collect tolls in this age is something wrong. It belongs to the dark ages, and should be abolished. I agree that it is a step in the wrong direction to collect tolls on any bridge in Prince Edward Island. We have no such savage remnant of the past In the whole province of Prince Edward Island.

I am very glad my hon. friend has come to my assistance. We have suffered a great deal from bridge tolls in the vicinity of Montreal, and we look upon them as an outrageous abuse-as a survival of the dark ages. We would like to abolish them, but my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has hitherto been an obstacle in the way. Willingly or unwillingly, he has not helped us as we expected he would to abolish these tolls. But I think we are entitled, before passing this item, to know what the arrangements are.

The arrangements are embodied in chapter 7 of 63-64 Victoria of the Statutes of Canada, confirming an agreement made between the Minister of Railways of Canada and the Commissioner of Public Works of the province of Prince Edward Island. Under that agreement the provincial government is to pay so much money yearly to the Dominion government, and is to have control of and keep in repair

the highway portion of the bridge, and to have the exclusive right to levy and collect tolls and charges for the use of the bridge if it desires to do so.

As I understand, the provincial government is not limited in its right to collect tolls, but can collect any amount it sees tit. In the vicinity of Montreal the amount of the tolls, at any rate, is limited. But I call my hon. friend's attention to this -and I do it very disinterestedly on the part of the people who will use that bridge 

that in connection with this bridge an abuse is being created which we have been trying to abolish in the neighbourhood of Montreal for over thirty years, and which was established there shortly after the conquest. We have had there the creation of a trust, and tolls have been exacted mercilessly from the people and have gone in great part to pay the expenses of the trustees and of the administration generally. My hon. friend will notice that the provincial government is merely obliged to "pay a certain fixed amount every year and to keep the wooden part of this bridge in repair. The bridge is certainly a work of general advantage to the people of Prince Edward Island. It has cost a great deal, and we have not finished paying for it yet. We have built it entirely at our own expense. It is therefore to be considered as a work for the general advantage of the Dominion. The obligation of the local government to keep the roadway planked and the wooden part of the bridge painted is very slight. I venture to say, from the experience that I have had, that that obligation in future will be largely lessened by the large amount of work which the federal government will have to perform upon that bridge. In the interest of the people of the island-and I am sure my hon. friend will support me in that-it will be a very great advantage to have that right of collecting tolls abolished and free circulation given to the people.
What is being done in connection with the Hillsboro bridge ? Is the work going on ?
Yes.
I have read in the newspapers that one of the piers has settled somewhat and got out of line and that the contractor was not able to go on with the work.
The newspaper was misinformed. He is going on with the work.

The case of the Montreal Turnpike Trust is not parallel with the one in question. The Montreal bridge is owned by a road company, but this bridge will be owned by the people of Prince Edward Island, and it is entirely in their hands whether they shall charge tolls or not.
So it is with us.

The people of Prince Edward Island will no doubt be pleased with the sympathy which the hon. gentleman shows in their affairs, but this matter is entirely in their own hands. The government will not levy a toll if the people do not wish it.
Does not my hon. friend think it would be a great advantage to the people who are going to use the bridge, to have the certainty that no toll will be charged ?
That will be a matter for the people themselves to decide.

In the neighbourhood of Montreal the roads are government roads. They are under the control of tfhe trusts who represent the government. On the Island of Montreal some of these trusts are appointed by the Minister of Finance and some by the local government; but as a matter of fact the roads to which I refer, and in connection with which the abuses I have condemned exist, are under the control of the people of the province of Quebec. It appears to me a pity that we should create an abuse among the people who are going to use this bridge. It would be better it should be a free bridge just as are the Interprovincial bridge here and others being built now.	.
Perhaps it will.
What makes my bon. friend think it will ? Had we not better, since wTe are paying for it, make sure of that now?
The province is paying for it.
Is the province contributing in any measure to the construction of the bridge ?
I do not want to split hairs. The province is paying the interest on the cost of that portion of the bridge.

Unless the bridge be built, the people of Prince Edward Island will have to continue their ferry, which has been in operation there for generations, at the expense of the people, and the ferry costs the people a much larger sum than would these tolls. It is a matter of provincial arrangement. The people, I presume, will know what is best in their own interest ; and as they are contributing a large amount, I do not see that we need worry ourselves about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In any case it is not the business of this government to supply free roads either to the people of Prince Edward Island or of Quebec. In this case the people of Prince Edward Island are giving a contribution which is supposed to represent , the interest on the cost of constructing that portion. And whether they charge tolls or not is a matter for themselves to determine. If they like to tax themselves, that is their business and not ours.
T

That is the old argument we hear every time we ask for relief for the province of Quebec. My hon. friend says it is not the business of the federal government to provide free roads for the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or any other province.

It is Unfortunate that he should argue in that way. He knows it is not our business either to lend money to the trustees of Montreal roads, but we have done that and we are to-day in this position, that we hold $200,000 of bonds of the Montreal Turnpike Trust on which the interest is not paid, and the masters of the situation are this government. The interest on those bonds has never been paid, and it is in the power of my hon. friend to say to the trustees of the Montreal roads and the local government : It is time this abuse shall cease and we are willing to forego our interest and the capital, provided the necessary reforms are made. Does my hon. friend pretend that when we are voting a sum of over $1,000,000 for the construction of a bridge, the whole cost of which we shall pay, it is not in our power to say : we will not vote that money unless there will be free circulation on the bridge for the people ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But my hon. friend overlooks the very important fact that we have already put in our conditions by a solemn agreement between this parliament and the parliament of Prince Edward Island. That agreement is signed, sealed and delivered. It suits t'he people of Prince Edward Island, and why we should be so anxious to prevent their paying tolls, I cannot understand. As to the Quebec case, we possibly have gone out of our way to lend money to the trustees of the Montreal turnpike road, but surely that is not an offence of which we should be accused. Surely my hon. friend does not consider that a crime.

No, but we stand in the position of a creditor who can impose on
his debtor what conditions he chooses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The one condition which my hon. friend is not willing to impose is that the debt should be paid or any part of it.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the debt is not collectable. I admit there is a distinction between the two cases, but it was only right that we should find out on behalf of the people of Prince Edward Island what are the conditions for the use of the bridge. There is an agreement in this case, but in that of the Montreal Turnpike there is none.

How much did we pay per mile for the building of the railway ? What was the contract price ? I understood the hon. minister to say that the whole road 191
was let by tender, but there is some doubt about it.
$4,621 per mile. That is exclusive of the bridge and of the wharf, that includes rails and equipment.
Was it all let by tender ?
Yes ; as I have explained.
That is surely not in keeping with the statements that have already been made to this House.
I have stated it as I have stated it.
You are not sure of your ground.
I have given the history of the matter just as I have now stated it.

Wrhat I understood from the minister is that the lowest tenderer was to nave got the contract, but the government judged that he was not fit to carry it out, and the next lowest tenderer was given the contract. Is that the case with the whole road ?

It was extended subsequently, as I stated before. The whole contract was given to the contractor who had received a portion of it at certain schedule rates, and it was continued to completion under that arangement.
When I asked if this was tendered for in two different parts, I understood the minister to say no.

I did not wish to convey a different impression from what I am Telling my hon. friend now. They only tendered for a portion of the road originally, but it was extended to the contract for the remaining portion.
Without tender ?
Without tender.
That is the truth ?
That is what I endeavoured to say.
The hon. gentleman said in the first place, and led us to believe, that it was given iby tender, when it was nothing of the kind.
I did not wish to convey that impression, because I had stated differently earlier in the evening. I had given the facts before just as I have given them now.

I understood the minister to say that the province pays $9,750 a year, which is supposed to be the interest upon the cost of the passenger traffic part of the bridge. Is that in perpetuity or for any definite length of time ?
It is unlimited.

We find that in many of these items the contracts are changed from



600S
the description given last year. The minister should tell us any changes that have been made since last year, if the contract has not been carried out on the same basis, for the same amount, and on the same principle ; and he should also tell us if the progress which has been made is commensurate with the original undertaking as to the completion of the contract at a definite period.
There is no change in the contract from what it was last year.
The same amount ?
The same rates are being paid this year as last.

The same rates ? I do not know whether the minister is designedly indefinite and thinks that that statement should satisfy the House, or whether he is innocently making indefinite statements. From his statements we cannot tell what kind of a contract has been entered into. Did the party who is now doing the whole work contract for a portion of it at schedule rates simply, and is he now working on schedule prices ?

I want to be clear, and to give the facts as they are. I do not know whether it is my fault in trying to explain these things or my hon. friend's fault in understanding it. What I wish to say is that Mr. Kitchen tendered for a portion of this line ; the line was from a certain point in Prince Edward Island to Murray Harbour.

And everything on
schedule prices ?

Everything was on schedule prices. Only a portion of the line was tendered for in the first instance. Subsequently the whole line to Murray Harbour was given to that same contractor on those same schedule prices.
Mr. SPROULEl	That might be very!
fair and might be very unfair. To illustrate, on some portion of the line the grading might be very difficult and on other portions very easy. There might be one kind of material in one place and another kind in another place.
They are paid according to the material.

The schedule prices being so much per cubic yard. Supposing you commence moving this material and are first moving the very easiest kind, and pay the contractors 25 cents a yard. If you come to a hard place it would be worth a great deal more, and in order to determine whether the contract was properly let or not we should have some information as to the character of the ground over which this railway is to be built, whether it is uniform and likely to be of uniform cost in different parts. We have no information in regard to that. A man might take a small piece of work where it was very heavy, and the schedule price would not be high ; but if he extend-Mr. SPROULE.
ed that same work into a locality where there was an easy soil and where he did not have to remove the material to as great a distance, then the price would be relatively very much higher. We ought to know all of this, in order to enable us to determine whether the contract is a reasonable one or not.
The schedule provides so much for rock, so much for earth and so much for other material, broken stone, etc.
Could the minister give us those prices ?
I made a return of that some time ago to parliament. I have not the contract here.
In connection with the bridge, I would ask the minister whether there is a contract for the building of the substructure only, or for the building of the whole bridge ?

There is one contract with Mr. Heney for the substructure and also a contract for the removal of the bridge from the Miramichi river to Prince Edward Island, and for the erecting of it on the substructure over the Hillsboro' river.
Who has the contract for the moving of the bridge ?
Mr. Hugh Macdonald. Mr. HACKETT. Will that bridge be quite wide enough to afford this carriage driveway alongside the railway, or will the bridge require to be extended ?
There is a sidewalk apart from the bridge as it now exists, and a carriage way will interlock with the railway proper, the bridge not being wide enough to have a separate track.
Will there be a carriage driveway on either side of the bridge ?
No, only on one side. Then there will be a passage for pedestrians, a sidewalk on both sides. That will be maintained by the local government.
Will this [DOT] bridge over the southwestern branch of the Mir imicin be quite sufficient to span the Hillsboro river ?

There are two Miramichi bridges, the northwest and the southwest. They proved to be too light for very heavy engines, and therefore they are being removed. We are taking all of the southwest bridge and a portion of the northwest, and utilizing them for bridging the Hillsboro river. The material is just as good as a new bridge would be purchased outright, because if you were to purchase one outright you could not get a heavier class of bridgte than the one you are now getting from the Miramichi.
What is the age of the bridge on the Miramichi river ?

The line was opened, I think, in 1876.

Prince Edward island Railway-New . station at Alberton, $2,000.

There were $3,000 provided last year, and the estimated expenditure during the year was $1,000. We require a revote of $2,000, and we shall still require to supplement this by $2,500 more. We are asking for tenders on three conditions, one to build in stone, one in brick and one in wood. The matter has not yet been finally determined, but I think it will be in favour of stone. The total cost will be about $4,500.	'
Is this a revote ?

It does not appear in the estimates that there has been anything expended at all. The $3,000 voted last year and the $2,000 this year will make $5,000. Perhaps this is a mistake in the estimates as printed.
Last year we did not expend anything.
Why don't you call it a revote ?

I have it marked here as a l-evote of $2,000. There appears to have been two or three errors of that kind made by tlie printers. They were not made in the Department of Railways and Canals. We estimated the expenditure in February last, and expected that the expenditure during the fiscal year ending June 30 would be $1,000, and we therefore ask for a revote of $2,000. But it is now found in view of the material that we will likely use, that we will require this $2,000. We have not expended a dollar of the vote of last year, and we will require $2,500 more, making a total expenditure at that point of $4,500.

We know the amount will be $4,500. But I understand the minister to say he has not expended a dollar of the usual vote given last year. Then that is wrong to begin with, and leaves a wrong impression upon the minds of the committee. Have you no proof reader to go over the amounts -after they are printed ?
We do not have anything to do with them. We send over our estimates to the Finance Department and they are sent forward to the Printing-Bureau. They do not come back to us.

I trust the minister will take some precaution to see that this does not occur again. Here we have
$2,000 when it ought to be $3,000, he should have asked a revote of $3,000. Then there is a mistake in the other column of $2,000 at all events. Now, there are various items showing the same error. It makes a material difference in testing what is the actual expenditure of the government.
I quite agree with my hon. friend.
Has any action been taken with regard to building this new station at Alberton ?	[DOT]
Tenders have been received, but the contract has not been awarded because we have not yet decided whether to use wood or stone.
I trust the minister will build a first-class station there.
We hope to.
Now, with regard to another matter. Has any action been taken to avoid the Y coming into that station ?
The matter is under consideration.
Have you a report on it from any of your officers ?
Yes, I have a report from the officer.
Will the hon. minister do what he possibly can to abate the nuisance ?
Yes, if it is possible to do so we will certainly do it.
Will t'his $4,500 ' complete the building including heating and lighting apparatus?
Everything. We believe that $4,500 will be the whole expenditure.
What proportion will go for heating and lighting ?
It will be heated by stoves. There will be no hot water system.

I understood the hon. minister to say that $4,500 is likely to be the full cost but he told us previously that he [DOT]bad an estimate for a building in wood, another in brick and another in stone. Which material did he contemplate using when he made up the estimate of $4,500 ?
I am basing that on the idea of utilizing stone.
If other material 'is used it will cost less ?
Yes.
There was an amount voted last year for building small stations at Richmond, Northam and Alberton. Are these works being proceeded with ?
Yes, they will be completed within the fiscal year.

The contracts 'have been let ?
<3011
Yes, months ago. The works are under contract and they have to he finished within the time to be paid out of the appropriation of last year.

The important thing is to have the accommodation for the people before the stormy weather commences in the fall of the year. I would like to liave that attended to.
Mr. EMMjERSON. They will have to be complete# now in order to be paid out of this appropriation.
Prince Edward Island Railway-Survey of Montague bridge, $500.
I would like to ask the minister what is the meaning of this item ?

Last year there was $2,000 provided. Here is where another error occurs in making up the estimates. This is a survey of a proposed branch line of railway and there was $1,500 expended on it up to the 30th June. That was the estimated amount and we anticipate that amount will be required. That leaves $500 uuexpended and we are asking for-ithis revote.
It should be marked ' revote.'
Yes. I think there have been four or five errors of that kind in the estimates.
What was the $1,500 expended on ?
In making a survey of this proposed branch of railway from Cardigan to Montague bridge.

I desire to bring to the notice of the hon. minister the building of a branch line of railway from O'Leary to the west shore of Prince Edward Island, about 12 miles in length. The hon. minister will remember that for several years past I have brought this matter up in this honourable House and that it has been received favourably by the government. I would like to ask him if he intends to have a survey made ?

That matter has already been brought to inv notice by the people of Prince Edward Island. Senator Yeo and others have presented petitions and made representations in reference to it. It is having the consideration of the department and I shall be very happy to announce any decision later on that may be reached in respect to the matter.

I asked a question myself in connection with this matter in the early part of the session and the hon. minister said then, about three months ago, that it was under consideration. He has been considering it ever since. I cannot get any definite answer from him. I have a resolution passed by the people of that section of the country who are suffering from the want of proper facilities for the transportation of their produce and other things. It is as follows :
At a meeting held in Springfield Hall, lot S, Prince Edward Island, on March 9th, 1904 for the purpose of discussing the question of a branch line from the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway to Cape Wolfe on the west shore-of the island, the following resolution was moved by Mr. W. J. 'Wortman,' seconded by Mr. Stephen McEachern, and carried unanimously, to be presented to the Minister of Railways through our representatives at Ottawa :*-[DOT]	'
To the Hon. H. R. Emmerson,
Minister of Railways, Ottawa.
May it please your Honour.
Whereas, a largely signed petition of the electors of townships No. 7, 8 and 9 praying for a branch line of railway from the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway at or near O'Leary station to Cape Wolfe on the west shore of the island, was forwarded to the Department of Railways during the session of 1903.
And whereas, the prayer of the petition has not received the consideration of the government.
Therefore, resolved, that the electors of townships No. 7, 8 and 9 desire to impress on the Minister of Railways the urgent needs of this section of the province, as stated in the petition of 1903, and the necessity of complying with the prayer of the said petition during the present session of parliament.
(Sgd.) W. T. COSTAIN, PETER J. BULGER	Chairman.
Secretary.
Springfield, lot 8, March 9. 1904.
I would like the hon. minister to do something to relieve these people in tlieir necessities as they present them in Phis resolution and as they have been shown by the petition sent to the hon. minister himself.
